conceptTag: Where to play, how to win
readerTitle: Target picked a country. It forgot to pick a way to win.
caseNote: 실제 기업 실패 사례 (Target Canada) + 가상 적용 (물류·창고 회사, 산업용 펌프 제조사, 일정 관리 소프트웨어)
insight: '어디서 경쟁할지'와 '거기서 어떻게 이길지'는 따로 고르는 두 결정이 아니라 한 쌍이다. 하나를 바꾸면 다른 하나도 다시 따져야 한다.
misconception: 크고 성장하는 시장을 고르면 전략은 거의 끝난 것이다. 또는 강점이 확실하면 어느 시장에서든 통한다.

sources.text: Lafley, A.G. & Martin, R. (2013). Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works. Harvard Business Review Press.
Target Corporation press release on discontinuing Canadian operations (January 2015)
Castaldo, J. (2016). The Last Days of Target. Canadian Business.

factChecks.note: Target Canada 첫 매장 개점 2013년 3월, 2013년 한 해 동안 약 124개 매장 개점, 2015년 1월 전 매장(약 133개) 폐점 발표. 카드에는 "more than 120 stores within about a year", "less than two years later"로 적었습니다. 게시 전 Target 보도자료로 재확인하세요.
실패 원인(재고 부족, 신규 물류·주문 시스템 문제, 미국 매장보다 높은 가격, Zellers 매장 부지 일괄 인수)은 Canadian Business(2016) 등 보도에 근거합니다. 손실 금액은 출처마다 달라 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
Lafley와 Martin이 P&G에서 함께 전략 작업을 했다는 내용은 Playing to Win 서문 기준입니다. 프레임워크 이름 대신 두 질문의 원리만 가르치도록 썼습니다.
물류 회사, 펌프 제조사, 일정 관리 소프트웨어 사례와 15% 할인, 10배 계약 규모 등의 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다.

cards.title: Target went to Canada. Canadians already loved it.
body: Many Canadians knew Target from shopping trips across the border. When it opened in Canada in 2013, it had a famous name, deep pockets and more than 120 stores within about a year.
Less than two years later, it announced it would close every one of them.

image.label: Empty store shelves under a bright red-and-white sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 넓고 밝은 대형 매장 안, 진열대 대부분이 비어 있고 쇼핑카트를 끄는 손님 한 명이 두리번거림. 매장 간판은 이름 없는 빨간 원형 표시로만. 실제 Target 로고·상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A new market opens up.
body: You run a regional freight and warehousing company. A large industrial park is being built two hours away, in a region where you have no customers. Three local carriers already serve it.
Your board wants a plan. What do you bring them?

options.text: Move in fast with your full service, before rivals sign the new tenants
options.feedback: You'd be first and visible. But speed of entry isn't a reason for tenants to pick you, and the local carriers already know the roads and the buyers.

options.text: Decide which tenants you'd serve there, and why they'd choose you over the locals
options.feedback: Slower to announce, but it answers both halves of a strategy: where you compete and what makes you win there.

options.text: Enter with prices 15% below the local carriers
options.feedback: Low price is a real way to win if your costs are lower too. If they aren't, you've bought customers you can't afford to keep.

cards.title: A place to play, but no plan to win there.
body: Target chose where to compete: all of Canada, almost at once. Its plan for winning there was thin.

Shoppers found empty shelves, because new warehouse and ordering systems struggled. Many found prices higher than at Target stores in the US. Most locations came from taking over another chain's store leases in one deal.
Canadians came expecting cheap, well-stocked, stylish stores. **The brand promised one thing and the stores delivered another.**

cards.title: Where to play, how to win
body: Every strategy answers two questions. **Where to play:** which customers, places, products and channels you'll compete for. **How to win:** why those customers will pick you over every alternative they have there.

A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin, who worked on strategy together at Procter & Gamble, built their approach around these two questions. The key is that they're *linked*. A reason to win only counts in a particular place.

image.label: Two interlocking puzzle pieces labeled Where and How
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 맞물리는 퍼즐 조각 두 개. 왼쪽 조각에 "Where to play"(지도 아이콘), 오른쪽 조각에 "How to win"(트로피 아이콘). 두 조각이 맞물리는 지점을 밝게 강조. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two answers, each with parts.
body: Where to play is a set of smaller choices:
list: **Customers:** who you serve, and who you don't
cards.callout: How to win usually takes one of two routes: serve those customers at lower cost than rivals, or offer something they value enough to choose you anyway. Target Canada had neither in place on day one.

cards.title: A strong way to win, in the wrong place.
body: Picture a maker of industrial pumps built to run for 20 years. That's a real edge with buyers who keep equipment for decades, like water utilities.
Now it chases fast-growing equipment rental fleets, which replace pumps every few years and buy on price. The same pump is suddenly too expensive, and its best feature is worth little.
Change where you play, and you have to check how you win all over again.

image.label: One sturdy pump facing two different buyers
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 가운데 튼튼한 산업용 펌프 하나. 왼쪽은 정수장 담당자가 엄지를 들고 "Lasts 20 years" 말풍선, 오른쪽은 렌탈 업체 직원이 가격표를 보며 고개를 저음. 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Clear choices have costs.
body: Choosing where to play means turning away customers outside it. That feels like lost revenue, and sometimes it is.
The choices also aren't permanent. Markets shift, and a place where you could win can stop being one. When pressure hits one answer, revisit both together.
And a list of target markets isn't a strategy until each one has a reason to win attached.

cards.title: Now it's software.
body: Your team sells appointment scheduling software. It wins with small dental clinics because it connects to the billing tools they already use.
A sales lead wants to go after hospitals, where deals are ten times bigger. What do you do?

options.text: Pursue hospitals with the current product and sales approach
options.feedback: Bigger deals, but hospitals run different billing systems and long buying processes. Your main reason to win doesn't travel with you.

options.text: First name what would make hospitals choose you, and whether you can build it
options.feedback: You may move slower, but you treat a new place to play as needing a new reason to win, which it does.

options.text: Stay with dental clinics and turn down every bigger lead
options.feedback: It protects what works today. But it rules out growth without checking whether you could earn a reason to win somewhere new.

cards.title: Choose where you'll compete and why you'll win there, together.
body: A big market without a reason to win is a trap. A real edge in the wrong market is wasted.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: "We serve [customers] in [place], and they choose us because [reason]." If the reason would work just as well for anyone, anywhere, it isn't one yet.
